articles.title_orig: Damage assessments, recovery ramp up after hurricane thrashes Florida Panhandle
articles.title_zh: Damage assessments, recovery ramp up after hurricane thrashes Florida Panhandle
articles.content_orig:
Live updates: Deadly post-tropical Isaias charges inland, unleashing vicious impacts on the South
Hurricane Isaias’ powerful landfall produced wind gusts of more than 115 mph across Florida, with a 118-mph gust recorded in Jay, according to a review of NWS storm reports by the FOX Forecast Center.
Top wind totals from Hurricane Isaias.
Oriole Beach recorded a 117-mph gust, followed by 116 mph at Santa Rosa Sound and 114 mph at Naval Air Station Whiting Field. Freeport also recorded a 110-mph gust as Isaias moved across the Florida Panhandle.
Flash Flood Warning in effect for parts of Georgia and South Carolina.
A Flash Flood Warning is in effect for portions of Georgia and South Carolina as heavy rainfall associated with Isaias continues to threaten communities across the Southeast.
The National Weather Service issued the warning at 4:36 p.m. EDT Saturday for portions of Burke, Columbia and Richmond counties in Georgia, along with Aiken and Edgefield counties in South Carolina. The warning remains in effect until 6:30 p.m. EDT.
Forecasters said 2 to 3 inches of rain have already fallen, with another 1 to 3 inches possible in the warned areas.
A tornado was also spotted Saturday night, but the warning has since expired.
The National Weather Service warned motorists not to drive through flooded roads or around barricades as dangerous flash flooding develops.
Hurricane Isaias’ destructive path has threatened more than lives and property, leaving wildlife and habitats vulnerable across Florida.
Storm surge and floodwaters can push manatees into shallow areas, canals, ponds and other locations where they may become stranded as water levels recede.
File photo. Credit: Florida Wildlife Conservation.
Florida wildlife officials are urging residents to avoid handling stranded, injured or dead manatees found after Hurricane Isaias and to report them to authorities instead.
The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said public safety remains its top priority before, during and after hurricanes and tropical storms.
Anyone who encounters a manatee in distress should keep their distance and call the FWC Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922. Residents should not attempt a wildlife rescue if doing so could place them in danger.
The FWC is working with partners across Florida to assess and address the storm’s impacts on wildlife populations and habitats.
Dramatic video captured west of Woods Crossroads, South Carolina, shows a tornado crossing Highway 301 as severe weather associated with Isaias sweeps across the Southeast.
The close-range footage captures the dangerous storm moving across the roadway, highlighting the ongoing tornado threat as Isaias pushes farther inland.
Hurricane Isaias washed out a section of road at Grayton Beach State Park in Florida, offering an early look at the storm’s damage along the Gulf Coast.
Hurricane Isaias damage at Grayton Beach State Park.
Florida State Parks staff were surveying parks across the state Saturday to assess damage from the hurricane and identify repairs needed before reopening.
Officials said the early assessments will help crews restore access and return the parks to visitors as quickly as possible.
The damage at Grayton Beach is one of the latest signs of Isaias’ impact along the Florida Panhandle, where powerful winds, heavy rain and storm surge battered coastal communities.
Hurricane Isaias forced the closure of at least 35 Florida state parks and associated overnight accommodations on Saturday across the Panhandle and Big Bend, as officials assess damage, clear debris and work to restore safe access.
For the latest information and a complete list of park closures, click here .
The flash flooding threat continues across the Southeast as post-tropical Cyclone Isaias moves through Alabama and toward the Southern Appalachians.
As of the 4 p.m. CDT (5 p.m. ET) advisory Saturday from the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center, Isaias was located about 5 miles west of Birmingham, Alabama.
The system was moving northeast at 15 mph with maximum sustained winds of 30 mph and a minimum central pressure of 1007 millibars.
Weather Prediction Center 5 p.m. ET advisory.
Despite losing its tropical characteristics, Isaias continues to produce heavy rain capable of triggering flash flooding across portions of the Southeast and Southern Appalachians.
The system is moving northeast at a steady pace, but additional rainfall could worsen flooding, especially in areas that have already received significant rain or where streams and rivers are elevated.
Flood Watches remain in effect for portions of the Southeast United States and Southern Appalachians.
A High Wind Warning is in effect for portions of the Southern Appalachians, while Wind Advisories cover portions of the Mid-South and Southern Appalachians.
Isaias was located about 180 miles south of Nashville, Tennessee, as of the latest advisory.
The post-tropical cyclone is expected to continue tracking northeast through the Southeast and Southern Appalachians, bringing the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and gusty winds along its path.
Dramatic video captured near Woods Crossroads, South Carolina, shows FOX Weather Exclusive Storm Tracker Brandon Copic's close-range encounter with a tornado as severe weather threatens the region.
The footage offers a striking look at the dangerous conditions unfolding across the Southeast as the region deals with storms associated with Isaias.
A confirmed tornado was reported Saturday afternoon in Allendale County, South Carolina, as severe thunderstorms moved through the region.
The National Weather Service in Charleston said the tornado was located over Appleton at 4:27 p.m. EDT and was moving north at 25 mph.
FOX Weather Exclusive Storm Tracker Brandon Copic is on the scene tracking severe storms across the Southeast.
The remnants of Isaias are supplying deep tropical moisture to the region, helping fuel slow-moving supercell thunderstorms capable of producing additional tornadoes.
A Tornado Watch is in place until 8 p.m. ET Saturday for portions of southeast Georgia and southeast South Carolina, including Allendale County, as severe thunderstorms capable of producing tornadoes moved through the region.
Hurricane Isaias left behind significant damage in Milton, Florida, after powerful winds battered the Gulf Coast Friday night. FOX News Correspondent Brandy Campbell reports from an apartment building that sustained major roof damage as the hurricane tore through the area.
The destruction is among the impacts being documented across the Florida Panhandle as residents begin assessing the damage left behind by Isaias.
Extensive damage is being reported in Pensacola, Florida, after Hurricane Isaias slammed the Gulf Coast Friday night with wind gusts topping 100 mph.
FOX Weather Correspondent Brandy Campbell surveyed the destruction, including an inn that had its roof torn off by the powerful winds.
The damage highlights the force of the hurricane as communities across the Florida Panhandle begin assessing the destruction and cleaning up in the storm's aftermath.
Thousands of additional utility workers are helping restore power across Alabama after Hurricane Isaias battered the Gulf Coast, leaving residents dealing with storm-related outages.
Alabama Power said 6,400 additional personnel from 25 states are working alongside its crews to restore electricity as quickly and safely as possible.
The utility said restoration efforts are ongoing and urged customers to check its outage map for the latest updates on power restoration.
The cleanup and recovery process is underway along Florida's Gulf Coast after Hurricane Isaias made landfall as a powerful Category 2 storm, leaving behind widespread damage.
FOX Weather Senior Correspondent Robert Ray captured video showing the aftermath in Pensacola Beach, Florida, where residents and emergency crews are beginning to assess the destruction left behind by the hurricane.

articles.title_orig: Tropical Storm Rachel is behaving in unusual ways. What that means for SoCal this weekend
articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Rachel is behaving in unusual ways. What that means for SoCal this weekend
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Tropical Storm Rachel brings with it  a slew of potential hazards, including damaging coastal flooding.
The National Hurricane Center warned that Rachel could pick up some strength before arriving on the West Coast — an unusual occurrence for storms in the tropical eastern Pacific.
Typically, storms weaken significantly once they enter those cooler waters. But El Niño conditions and an ongoing marine heat wave have pushed ocean temperatures 10 to 13 degrees higher than normal, providing a far-more-conducive environment for Rachel.
“It’s notable that this is an unusual event that’s being made possible by both coincidence of this early arriving low-pressure trough off the coast of California and the record warm — and I do mean record warm — ocean temperatures off the coast of California right now,” UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain said during a briefing  Friday.
Rachel is expected to make landfall either in northern Baja California or San Diego County as early as Saturday night.
In the modern record, only two storms  have passed through the state at tropical-storm strength.
The first — nicknamed El Cordonazo, or the Lash of St. Francis — hit Long Beach and San Pedro in September 1939 . It dumped 5.62 inches of rain on L.A. over three days, spawned wind gusts of up to 65 mph and resulted in 45 deaths from flooding, with an additional 48 deaths at sea.
There was also Nora in September 1997, which was briefly at tropical storm strength as its center passed along the California-Arizona border, but California was spared the kind of damage it delivered to Baja California. Street flooding was reported in Imperial County, the Coachella Valley and San Diego, while big waves boosted by Nora and another storm sent breakers crashing into beachfront properties in Seal Beach, seriously damaging three homes and resulting in minor damage to 45 others.
The blistering heat that has baked Southern California for days is coming to an end, with rain on tap for the weekend and early next week, along with a risk of potentially damaging coastal flooding.
The National Weather Service office in San Diego on Friday issued a rare tropical storm watch for most of San Diego County, including San Diego, Chula Vista, Carlsbad and Oceanside, meaning that tropical storm-force winds are possible over the next 48 hours. It’s only the second time a tropical storm watch has  been issued in California.
Coastal flooding will remain the biggest concern for the region in the coming days, particularly for south-facing shores, given the combination of high tides, a higher-than-typical water level and the arriving tropical storm. Swells will not only bring the potential for water intrusion, but also hazardous surf — ranging from 3 to 6 feet in some areas — and rip currents, according to the weather service.
Officials had predicted that tides in Southern California would be 1 foot to 1.5 feet above normal what would ordinarily be expected without the abnormally warm ocean temperatures wrought by El Niño .
Around 9 a.m. Friday, the high tide in San Diego and La Jolla was coming in 17 inches higher than the official prediction, which doesn’t account for hotter-than-normal ocean waters or swells from tropical storms, according to NOAA’s tide forecasts. Tides were coming in 16 inches higher than the official prediction in Santa Monica and 14 inches higher in San Francisco as of Friday morning.
“We’ve got water that’s already high and then we’re going to have periods of high tides each morning and evening and then on top of that we have high surf,” said Miguel Miller, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in San Diego. “We have all these things stacking up on each other and we’ve already seen in recent weeks how just the high tides, even without the large surf, is putting water into places where it doesn’t usually go.”
Forecasters are warning that south-facing beaches in Southern California could be particularly at risk of flooding on account of Tropical Storm Rachel this weekend.
A coastal flood advisory for Ventura, Los Angeles, Orange and San Diego counties — warning of the potential for flooding in beach parking lots, boardwalks and roads, with isolated road closures expected, along with minor coastal erosion — is expected to remain in effect through Tuesday afternoon.
Coastal cities including Laguna Beach, Newport Beach and Long Beach have already seen significant flooding. Long Beach issued a mandatory evacuation order for residents of Seaside Walk between 64th and 66th Place.
While tropical moisture from the remnants of Rachel is expected to deliver only light rain to much of Southern California between Sunday morning and Monday night, the Mojave Desert, the Inland Empire and portions of San Diego County could see more significant precipitation.
The weather service is warning that there is a moderate, or 40% chance, of excessive rainfall that could lead to flash flooding in places like San Diego, El Cajon, Chula Vista, Escondido, Palm Springs and Twentynine Palms. A moderate risk means that numerous flash floods are likely, and that many streams may flood. There is a chance that the San Diego River near Fashion Valley could reach minor flood stage.
There’s also a 15% chance of that occurring in Oceanside, San Clemente, Laguna Niguel, Riverside, San Bernardino, Las Vegas and the California-Arizona border; and a 5% chance in places like Huntington Beach, Santa Ana, Long Beach, Anaheim, Pomona, Victorville, Barstow, and most of Arizona and southern Utah.
Newport Beach was one of several coastal communities to see flooding Friday as residents braced for Tropical Storm Rachel, which is expected to cause more issues over the weekend.
In Los Angeles County, rain is expected to be light to moderate, ranging from about a quarter of an inch to an inch across much of the region. A bit more rain is expected in the San Gabriel Mountains, according to the weather service office in Oxnard. Rain rates are probably going to be a quarter of an inch per hour or less, making debris flow and landslides unlikely.
A bit more rain is expected in Orange County with coastal areas receiving from half an inch to an inch over the weekend and into early next week. Coastal sections of San Diego County could see between an inch and an inch and a half of precipitation with higher rain levels predicted farther inland.
Nora arrived during a “very strong” El Niño season. That pattern is linked to above-average hurricane activity in the eastern Pacific, and also is usually tied to above-average rainfall for Southern California in the winter.
That climate pattern sees the heating of ocean waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, which spur changes in the atmosphere that can affect weather around the world.
Strong surf across Southern California this weekend blasted through a seawall in Long Beach, caused a massive sinkhole at a celebrity’s Malibu home and damaged several Dana Point homes, among other issues.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center said  Thursday that there is virtually a 100% chance that the El Niño this season will be categorized as “very strong.” There’s also an 83% chance that this El Niño will be the strongest on record, which goes back to 1950, up from a 75% probability forecast last month.
“With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed,” the Climate Prediction Center said Thursday.
There have been only four “very strong” El Niños in the modern record — 1982-83, 1991-92, 1997-98 and 2015-16. Two of them — in 1982-83 and 1997-98 — deluged downtown Los Angeles with more than 30 inches of rain, more than double the area’s average annual rainfall.

articles.title_orig: China, EU talks show scope for cooperation despite disputes: expert
articles.title_zh: China, EU talks show scope for cooperation despite disputes: expert
articles.content_orig:

By continuing to browse our site you agree to our use of cookies, revised Privacy Policy and Terms of Use. You can change your cookie settings through your browser.
China and the European Union have the potential to deepen economic and trade cooperation by addressing their differences through negotiations and providing businesses with a more stable and predictable environment, a Chinese trade expert told CGTN on Saturday, following the two sides' latest trade talks in Beijing.
The remarks followed the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, co-chaired by Chinese Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao and European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic in Beijing from Thursday to Friday. A joint statement released on Friday said the two sides had agreed to maintain stable bilateral economic and trade ties and make them more balanced.
"The statement has made it very clear that both sides agree that we are going to negotiate in a better way," said Zhou Mi, a senior research fellow at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation.
China and the EU have complementary advantages in markets, innovation and businesses, Zhou said, adding that the two sides could better address uncertainties and restrictions through dialogue.
He said policy stability and predictability were crucial to encouraging businesses to invest and expand cooperation. "When enterprises are going to make investments, they have to understand that the situation will be stable."
Supply chains and industrial chains are built on collaboration and trust, Zhou said, adding that businesses would be more willing to strengthen ties if they believed cooperation would bring them further opportunities.
The joint statement outlined 16 areas of consensus, covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization (WTO) reform. The two sides also agreed to continue exploring the possibility of reducing tariffs on certain goods within the framework of WTO rules and reached an understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles.
Zhou said China and the EU could help restore confidence in global trade governance amid growing uncertainty and protectionism.
China and the EU are firm supporters of globalization, he said, calling for stronger support for the multilateral trading system, including through improvements to dispute settlement and efforts to address emerging issues such as e-commerce.
The two sides also identified potential cooperation in artificial intelligence, the digital economy and new energy. Zhou said turning that potential into concrete business and investment opportunities would depend partly on whether companies had confidence in policy stability and the prospects for cooperation.
China and the EU agreed to hold their next meeting under the trade and investment consultation mechanism in March 2027, with a ministerial video conference scheduled for January. Both sides also agreed to maintain close communication and promote the early implementation of the agreed outcomes.

articles.title_orig: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
articles.title_zh: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
articles.content_orig:
As the Trump administration announced Thursday that it suspended eight tech companies from sponsoring foreign workers for green cards, Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft , claiming it replaced the 6,000 workers it laid off in 2025 with people on H-1B work visas.
The suspension of the Labor Department's PERM program for green cards, which grant permanent residency to immigrants, doesn't affect H-1Bs, which are temporary work permits, but H-1B approval data shows how heavily these companies rely on foreign workers.
Data from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' H-1B Employer Data Hub also shows that Amazon and Meta were the biggest sponsors of H-1B visas, and neither was suspended.
The crackdown went beyond tech. At the same news conference Thursday, the Labor Department's inspector general, Anthony D'Esposito, announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities. Trump supporters have long argued that these programs undercut American workers by incentivizing employers to hire from abroad.
All eight suspended companies rank among the nation's top 50 H-1B sponsors. Most are IT services and consulting firms. Adobe is the smallest, at No. 45.
Amazon, with 19,178 H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025, and Meta, with 6,294, were the top two sponsors, and neither was suspended. Microsoft was a close third with 6,258, according to the USCIS data hub. Microsoft out-sponsored Amazon for years. Amazon passed Microsoft in 2017 and now gets about three times as many approvals.
The numbers cut both ways. Microsoft did receive more than 6,000 H-1B approvals last year, as Vance said. But 2 in 3 went to people already working there. Amazon, which brought in nearly four times as many H-1B workers new to the company, was not on the suspension list.

articles.title_orig: One year on, Gaza ceasefire exists ‘in name only,’ aid groups say amid near-daily Israeli strikes
articles.title_zh: One year on, Gaza ceasefire exists ‘in name only,’ aid groups say amid near-daily Israeli strikes
articles.content_orig:
A Palestinian mother mourns her son, who was killed in an Israeli airstrike just over a month into the ceasefire, at Al-Shifa Hospital, in Gaza City, on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Editor's note: This story contains graphic images of violence and death.
GAZA STRIP — President Donald Trump promised an end to Israel's war in Gaza after he pushed Israel to agree to a ceasefire and Hamas to release remaining Israeli hostages. The deal came into effect on Oct. 10, 2025.
A year later, however, there's still no international peacekeeping force in Gaza as promised and no reconstruction. Instead, Israel's military has expanded its control to roughly 70% of Gaza, squeezing more than 2 million Palestinians near the sea's edge.
Israel has also continued targeting Hamas throughout the ceasefire. Those attacks have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians this past year, nearly 500 of them women and children, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
Although the bombings have not stopped, they have slowed down during the ceasefire.
That has given people in Gaza a chance to recover from what U.N.-backed experts declared was a famine in the north of the territory last year. More food is now entering, reversing starvation across Gaza.
NPR's reporter in Gaza, Anas Baba, has been capturing moments of respite and continuous grief over the past 12 months of the ceasefire. Below are a selection of his photos.
Palestinians returned to the ruins of Gaza City after Israeli forces withdrew and ended their ground operation on the first day of the ceasefire, on Oct. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
In Khan Younis, families greet Palestinian prisoners who were freed in exchange for Israeli hostages on Oct. 13, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
At Al-Shifa Hospital on Oct. 23, 2025, Joud Al-Angar, 12, and his younger cousin are covered in dime-sized scabs after they were wounded by a piece of shrapnel from an Israeli munition. They found it in the rubble and thought it was coal they could use to help their family cook dinner. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
The bodies of multiple people, including children, are covered in shrouds at a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital on Nov. 20, 2025, after Israeli airstrikes targeted homes and tents. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
People inspect the aftermath of a deadly Israeli airstrike that destroyed a home in Gaza City six weeks into the ceasefire on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A father and his son wade through flooded streets in Gaza City after picking up humanitarian aid on Nov. 25, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Children wear virtual reality headsets as part of a TechMed Gaza initiative that aims to help provide children with psychosocial support for trauma, in Al-Zuweida, Gaza, on Dec. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Saqer Al-Ankah holds his dying 10-year-old granddaughter, Bayan, in his arms at Baptist Hospital in Gaza City on Dec. 10, 2025, after she was shot in her tent by Israeli troops who occupy northeast Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Makeshift tents like these in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025, offer little protection from the winter cold, but the U.N. says roughly 1.5 million people have only these for shelter after Israeli airstrikes destroyed nearly all the buildings in the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Raed el-Ghazawi and his children stand in a tent in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025. The family of five says the tent is freezing cold and damp from winter rainstorms. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
On Dec. 17, 2025, Palestinian Christian children decorate a Christmas tree inside the Holy Family Church in Gaza City for the first time since the beginning of the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Fresh produce returns to Gaza City's streets on Dec. 23, 2025, after U.N.-backed experts declared a famine there amid Israeli restrictions on aid during the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Patients sit in a clinic run by Doctors Without Borders in Gaza City on Dec. 31, 2025, a day before Israel banned more than 40 international aid organizations from bringing in staff or aid to Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian female artists gather at the beach in Gaza City for the first time since the war began to paint as a form of therapy, on Feb. 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian rescue workers begin the work of retrieving corpses from under the rubble of homes bombed by Israel during the war in Beit Lahia, Gaza, on Feb. 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
The skeleton of Shawqi Abu Naser, 60, is retrieved from under the rubble on Feb. 16, 2026, more than a year after an Israeli airstrike killed 132 people from the same family in Beit Lahia. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A mother from the Abu Nasr family sits by her son's body in Beit Lahia on Feb. 17, 2026. The body was retrieved from under the rubble more than a year after 132 people were killed in a single Israeli airstrike on the family home. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinians gather in an open space in Gaza City for early morning prayers that mark the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child smiles next to a man dressed as a clown on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, celebrations that mark the end of Ramadan fasting, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian boy shakes hands with Hamas militants on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, following the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinians stand next to boxes of U.N. food aid in an area that aid groups need Israeli permission to enter in Jabalia, Gaza, on April 18, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A yellow block placed by Israeli forces marks the expanding territory controlled by the military in Bureij, Gaza, on May 7, 2026. Palestinians are barred from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Young Palestinian chess players gather at a coffee shop in Gaza City for the first tournament since the start of the war, on May 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian child carries jugs of water as he passes by a mural of Spanish soccer star Lamine Yamal that is painted on the rubble of a home destroyed by Israeli airstrikes, in Al-Shati refugee camp, Gaza, on May 14, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A building burns after an Israeli airstrike killed Izz al-Din al-Haddad, the leader of the military wing of Hamas, his wife, his daughter and a neighbor in Gaza City on May 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Children jump on a trampoline during the Eid holidays on May 31, 2026, in Beit Lahia, which the Israeli military had deemed an "orange zone." Aid organizations are restricted from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child looks into a burned car that was targeted in an Israeli airstrike on a busy street in Gaza City on June 22, 2026. A teenage girl who was going to find internet access to take her final exams was killed in the strike. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A plume of smoke rises after an Israeli airstrike targeted a home in Gaza City nine months into the ceasefire on July 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Thousands of displaced Palestinians gather under Egyptian flags amid the rubble in Gaza City for a public screening of Egypt's match against Argentina in the World Cup on July 7, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
One-hundred corpses are wrapped in Palestinian flags in Gaza City on Aug. 4, 2026, after being retrieved from under the rubble of a building that was hit in an Israeli airstrike in October 2023. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian child whose brother was killed in an Israeli airstrike cries at the door of a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City on Aug. 19, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian children form a chain for a global solidarity initiative called Swim With Gaza that raises money for swimming lessons in Khan Younis on Aug. 25, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child's toys are stained with blood in Gaza City

articles.title_orig: Palestinian Authority president postpones legislative elections another year, marking 20 years without a vote
articles.title_zh: Palestinian Authority president postpones legislative elections another year, marking 20 years without a vote
articles.content_orig:
President Mahmoud Abbas postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree on Friday to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council almost another year.
Rather than take place as scheduled next month, the decree pushes the elections back to Sept. 11, 2027, according to WAFA, the official Palestinian news agency. Presidential elections, which have not taken place for more than two decades, are scheduled for the same day.
The postponement leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority's credibility among ordinary Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.
The internationally backed body is dominated by Abbas' party, Fatah, and has administered semiautonomous parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank since agreements reached in the 1990s. It has grown increasingly unpopular throughout Abbas' presidency. Many Palestinians view it as corrupt and criticize its security cooperation with Israel.
The decree came after a committee of top Palestinian officials met Saturday morning to discuss postponing the vote. The Palestine Liberation Organization's Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, noting that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.
The move was expected after Palestinian factions across the political spectrum met in Cairo for discussions on delaying the vote, Islamic Jihad deputy secretary-general Mohammed al-Hindi told The Associated Press earlier this week.
Palestinians have not held a legislative election since 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries then boycotted its government, fueling months of unrest that led to the Hamas takeover of Gaza the following year. Power has been divided between Gaza and the West Bank in the two decades since, with Hamas in control of Gaza and Abbas' Palestinian Authority in power in the West Bank.
The West Bank has grown increasingly violent in recent years as Israel has expanded settlements and outposts. Settler attacks on Palestinians and Israeli army raids on cities under the authority's control are both regularly reported.
Though the U.S.-brokered ceasefire plan reached last year outlined a future role for the authority, its immediate role was left mostly undefined as Hamas has continued to govern and the technocrats under the Board of Peace remain in Cairo awaiting permission to enter Gaza to transition power.
Before the postponement, leading factions had not registered slates to contest the election. But behind the scenes, veteran officials had been in talks to join forces and take aim at Abbas. An unlikely alliance had emerged between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and a bloc led by former Fatah security chief Mohammed Dahlan. Dahlan had previously been driven from Gaza by Hamas and was exiled in 2010 after a falling-out with Abbas.
"Abbas is terrified by the electoral alliance bringing our faction together with opposition factions and forces within Fatah that reject his leadership," Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan's faction, said in a statement.
Abbas has served as president since 2005 and delayed several presidential and legislative elections throughout his tenure.

articles.title_orig: AI euphoria faces concern as bubble warnings intensify (OPENAI:Private)
articles.title_zh: AI euphoria faces concern as bubble warnings intensify (OPENAI:Private)
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
It's not easy being a billionaire in the event that a stock market bubble bursts.
Just ask billionaire Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio, who sounds like he's worrying about potentially massive wealth destruction if the artificial intelligence trade goes south.
"Everybody says 'I'm worth a billion dollars' but, OK, try to spend that," Dalio said at the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore on Wednesday. Bloomberg first reported his comments.
Dalio suggested that measures that force the ultrawealthy to liquidate their unrealized gains, such as a wealth tax, could hasten or contribute to a bubble popping.
"In order to spend that, you have to sell wealth in order to get money — and so the bubble usually pricks at that," he added.
Read more: How billionaires get away with paying less income tax
Dalio warned that AI speculation may be nearing its peak. "We're in the part of the cycle that is before that but approaching that," Dalio said on the bubble topic. "I think we're close to that."
To his point, the stock market is pretty much being kept afloat by three tech stocks , which is fueling fresh fears of an AI stock bubble bursting.
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) has never been more concentrated in just three stocks than it is today, with Nvidia ( NVDA ), Apple ( AAPL ), and Microsoft ( MSFT ) representing over 21% of the index, per data from Creative Planning.
The importance of these three stocks to the S&P 500 has never been greater.
Only IBM ( IBM ), AT&T ( T ), and ExxonMobil ( XOM ) could hold a candle to the three tech stalwarts of today: In the mid-1980s, those three industrial giants at their peak made up 13.4% of the S&P 500.
We hope Dalio has his finances in order, should that bubble burst.
